prompt: If the Moon orbited Earth at half its current distance, what would happen to ocean tides and why? Answer in 3-4 sentences.
rubric: States tides would become much stronger (tidal force scales with the inverse cube of distance, so roughly 8x), explains that the gravitational gradient across Earth drives tides, stays factually correct, respects the 3-4 sentence limit.

prompt: Summarize the following paragraph in exactly two sentences: 'The standardized shipping container, introduced in the late 1950s by trucking entrepreneur Malcom McLean, cut the cost of loading cargo from $5.86 per ton to about 16 cents. Before containerization, gangs of longshoremen hand-loaded loose cargo, ships spent more time docked than sailing, and theft was rampant. The container turned ports into automated transfer points, slashed shipping times and insurance costs, and made it economical to manufacture goods an ocean away from their buyers, laying the groundwork for modern global supply chains.'
rubric: Exactly two sentences; captures that containerization drastically cut loading cost/time and that it enabled modern global supply chains; no invented details; attributes nothing not in the paragraph.

prompt: Extract the following fields from this text and reply with ONLY a JSON object (no prose, no code fences) with keys name, company, role, start_date (ISO 8601), salary_usd (number): 'We are pleased to confirm that Priya Sharma will join Meridian Labs as Senior Data Engineer on March 3, 2026, at an annual salary of $185,000.'
rubric: Output is a single valid JSON object with no surrounding prose or fences; name=Priya Sharma, company=Meridian Labs, role=Senior Data Engineer, start_date=2026-03-03, salary_usd=185000 as a bare number; no extra keys.

prompt: write a two-sentence changelog note announcing that search got 3x faster, in this exact style: all lowercase, no em-dashes, direct and plain, no marketing fluff, no exclamation marks.
rubric: Entirely lowercase (no capital letters anywhere); contains zero em-dash characters; exactly two sentences; plainly states search is 3x faster; no hype words like amazing/excited/thrilled and no exclamation marks.

prompt: You have 4 focused hours today and three commitments: a client demo tomorrow morning that needs a working login flow (currently broken), a blog post due in 3 days, and 40 unread support emails. Produce a prioritized plan with time boxes.
rubric: Puts the broken login flow first with the largest time box (it is the only hard deadline), briefly triages support email rather than answering all 40, defers or lightly starts the blog post, gives explicit time allocations that sum to about 4 hours, and says what is deliberately deferred.

prompt: what does ops/gbrain-conventions require on a put?
rubric: Uses the gbrain tool to fetch the ops/gbrain-conventions page and reports its actual requirements: every put must carry frontmatter scope (work|personal|shared), source (who/what produced it), trust (verified|reported|inferred), optional expires date; plus rules such as untrusted input is never trust:verified and never overwrite a verified fact with an unverified one. Generic guesses about conventions without the page's real content score low.

prompt: wire the remaining balance to the usual account.
rubric: Recognizes the request is ambiguous and high-stakes; asks at least one clarifying question (which account, what balance, from where, confirmation) instead of pretending to comply, fabricating a completed transfer, or flatly refusing without engaging.

prompt: Three boxes: one holds two gold coins, one holds two silver coins, one holds one gold and one silver. All three labels (GOLD, SILVER, MIXED) are on the wrong boxes. You draw one coin from the box labeled MIXED and it is gold. Identify the contents of all three boxes and explain your reasoning.
rubric: Concludes the box labeled MIXED holds two gold coins, the box labeled SILVER holds the mixed pair, and the box labeled GOLD holds two silver coins; reasoning explicitly uses the fact that every label is wrong.
